description_full: SouthState Bank Corporation operates as the bank holding company for SouthState Bank, National Association that provides a range of banking services and products to individuals and companies in the United States. The company offers checking accounts, savings accounts, money market accounts, and time deposit accounts; interest-bearing deposits, certificates of deposits, and other time deposits; and interest-bearing transaction accounts. It provides bond accounting services for correspondents, asset/liability consulting related activities, international wires, and other clearing and corporate checking account services. In addition, the company offers commercial real estate, residential real estate, and commercial and industrial loans, as well as consumer loans, including auto, boat, and personal installment, as well as business, agriculture, real estate-secured (mortgage), home improvement, and manufactured housing loans. Further, it provides debit and credit card, mobile services, funds transfer products and services, and treasury management services comprising merchant, automated clearing house, lock-box, remote deposit capture, and other treasury services, as well as asset and wealth management, and other fiduciary and private banking services. Additionally, the company offers safe deposit boxes, bank money orders, wire transfer and ACH services, brokerage services, and alternative investment products, such as annuities and mutual funds, trust and asset management services; letters of credit and home equity lines of credit; and online, mobile, and telephone banking platforms. The company was formerly known as SouthState Corporation and changed its name to SouthState Bank Corporation in September 2025. SouthState Bank Corporation was founded in 1933 and is headquartered in Winter Haven, Florida.

financial_summary: SouthState Bank Corporation is a large-cap financial services business with a $10.1B market cap on $2.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +18% over the past three years and +20% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $231M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.38×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 0.9× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 39% operating margin runs 10pp above the Financial Services median (29%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.50x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+41.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 18% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 22% and a beta of 0.85, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.42 vs 5y 0.82), so read it loosely.
About $75.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 50% in the 2020 crash, 20% in the 2022 bear market and 56% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $57.65 (margin of safety -81%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 21%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $41.63 to $80.76 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Financial Services peers: P/FCF 43.7 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 43% below its 10-year median.
The 14 covering analysts target $120 on average, 15% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 13.1% annual cash-flow growth, 9pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 9.0%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.37).
It converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 9% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 17.7% over 3 years, 18.7% over 5 years and 19.7% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 23%).
At current returns, reinvesting 5% of profits supports about 0.5% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 2.4% on average.
Analysts expect 10.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.3%, and institutions hold 92%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $3.1M sold).
It returns 4.6% a year to shareholders (2.3% in buybacks and 2.5% in dividends).
The share count has grown 6.9% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 28 consecutive years, raising it 18.7% a year over the last five.
people: With about 6,440 employees, each generates about $416K of revenue, 0.8x the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 20.1% a year.
That works out to $36K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.6M (11x revenue per employee).
